candidate_relations.reason: Biopsy shows thickened collagen, fibroblast activation, and lymphocytic perivascular inflammation without vessel-wall destruction, making carboplatin vasculitis incompatible.
The symmetric sclerotic edema lacks purpura and histologic leukocytoclastic or necrotizing vasculitis despite carboplatin exposure.
Pembrolizumab could cause scleroderma-like toxicity, but onset after pemetrexed maintenance and the reference attribution to pemetrexed make the proposed drug cause incompatible.
Acute painful bilateral shin edema beginning five days after chemotherapy is unlike idiopathic morphea, even though dermal collagen thickening creates a sclerotic resemblance.
The candidate assigns pembrolizumab and secondary lipodermatosclerosis, whereas the record shows an acute post-pemetrexed event without evidence of chronic venous disease.
Pemetrexed exposure and five-day latency support a pemetrexed skin reaction, but this label omits the distinctive inflammatory edema evolving into sclerotic plaques.
Indurated plaques and thickened dermal collagen fit a scleroderma-like reaction, but the label lacks the inflammatory edema phase and pemetrexed cause.
The bilateral post-treatment sclerosis fits a chemotherapy-induced scleroderma-like reaction, but the candidate does not identify pemetrexed or the edema-predominant presentation.
The biopsy did not show septal panniculitis or Miescher granulomas, and the clinical lesions were diffuse sclerotic plaques rather than tender nodules.
The close temporal relationship to maintenance chemotherapy supports cutaneous toxicity, but this umbrella diagnosis lacks the causal agent and inflammatory-sclerotic edema phenotype.
Lipodermatosclerosis generally reflects chronic venous hypertension, while this patient had abrupt symmetric plaques after chemotherapy and no documented venous insufficiency.
Lymphocytic inflammation is present, but immune-mediated dermatitis does not explain the marked edema, collagen sclerosis, and drug-specific timing.
Simultaneous bilateral lower-leg swelling five days after a chemotherapy cycle points to a drug reaction rather than spontaneous morphea.
The biopsy describes dermal collagen and perivascular lymphocytes without panniculitis, and the proposed pembrolizumab cause conflicts with the pemetrexed attribution.
Symmetric involvement, absence of fever, normal leukocyte count and CRP, and sclerotic histology argue strongly against cellulitis.
Pemetrexed is the relevant drug, but no purpura or histologic vessel injury supports cutaneous vasculitis.
There is no livedo, ulceration, thrombosis, or ischemic histology; instead the specimen shows collagen thickening and activated fibroblasts.
The edema arose abruptly after cycle eight and Doppler excluded thrombosis, with no chronic stasis signs described to support venous insufficiency.
No eosinophilia or fascial biopsy abnormality is reported, and histology localizes the process to thickened dermal collagen.
Chemotherapy-related leg dermatitis captures treatment timing and site, but omits pemetrexed attribution and the inflammatory-to-sclerotic edema evolution.

case_quality_flags: concurrent pembrolizumab exposure limits certainty of single-drug attribution
